transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, they sent me here from the station. I was... I was moving the airway bags into a pattern. I just knew it was the right pattern, the way they had to sit. Airway bags are heavier than they look, actually. We use the blue ones mostly, but they tried giving us these cheap green ones last year that had zippers that always got stuck. I hate when zippers stick, especially when it's raining out on a call and your gloves are wet. 

But yeah, I was moving them, putting them in the pattern and repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Just saying them. And my lieutenant told me to stop. He told me to step away. He’s this guy who always wears his boots too tight, squeaks every time he walks down the hall, it drives everybody crazy. But I wouldn't step away. I couldn't do it. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. Just completely bad. Like when you leave meat out on the counter too long and it gets that sweet kind of rot smell. My neighbor cooks meat like that sometimes and the smell comes right through the vents in my apartment, I keep meaning to call the landlord about the ventilation... but yeah, that's why they sent me here.
Did you feel like you had to put the airway bags in that specific pattern?

Yeah, I had to. I had to put them in the pattern. If I didn't, like I said, the whole bay would just... it would go bad. It's a feeling you get, you know? Like when you just know something is off. The sequence had to be right, and I had to keep saying the dispatch numbers out loud to lock it in. 

Dispatch numbers are funny, actually. They always start with the same three digits for our district, 4-1-9. 419... kind of like that area code in Ohio. I drove through Ohio once, years ago. Flat. So flat you could see the weather coming from a mile away. We stopped at this diner and I had the best cherry pie I've ever eaten in my life. The crust was really flaky, not like that soggy stuff you get at the grocery store. I don't know why people even buy grocery store pie when it's just going to disappoint them. 

But yeah, my lieutenant, he just didn't get it. He told me to stop and step away, but I couldn't. I couldn't break the sequence. If I stopped moving the bags and stopped saying the numbers, everything would just... rot.
Did you feel like you would have a bad thought or something bad would happen if you didn't put the airway bags in that specific pattern?

Yeah, exactly, like I just said a minute ago... if I didn't keep the bags in the pattern and keep saying the numbers, the whole bay would go bad. It would just rot. That's why I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant kept telling me to stop. I couldn't. I had to finish the sequence. 

The bay is where we park the rigs, you know, and the concrete floors out there... they get so incredibly slick when we wash the ambulances. We use this industrial soap that comes in these massive yellow drums. Yellow is a really aggressive color, if you think about it. Like school buses. I rode bus 42 in middle school. The driver, Mr. Henderson, he always listened to AM talk radio. Just static and people complaining about the mayor or the potholes. I never understood why people call into radio stations. Do they think anyone is actually listening? Like, really listening to them? My phone battery always dies if I talk on it too long anyway. 

But anyway... yeah, I had to keep the sequence going with the bags. I couldn't just stop.
Did you think that not putting the airway bags in the pattern would actually cause something bad to happen, or was it just a feeling you couldn't shake?

I mean, I keep telling you, it wasn't just some feeling in my head. It would actually happen. The whole bay would physically rot. That's why I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant kept telling me to stop. I had to keep moving the airway bags into that exact pattern and repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, or the rot would just... start. 

You can't just leave things unfinished. Like the milk in the station fridge. We get it in these heavy glass bottles from a local dairy. Glass is so much better than plastic because plastic makes everything taste like chemicals. My uncle worked at a chemical plant in Jersey for a while. He had to wear this bright orange jumpsuit with reflective tape all over it. Reflective tape is impossible to peel off once it's stuck to something. I tried peeling an old inspection sticker off my locker and it just left all this sticky white residue everywhere. You really need rubbing alcohol to get that stuff off. We carry rubbing alcohol on the rig, obviously, but... anyway, yeah, I couldn't stop. I had to finish the sequence so the bay wouldn't go bad.
Do you think other people would understand why the bay would rot if you didn't put the airway bags in that specific pattern?

I don't know if they'd understand. I mean, my lieutenant obviously didn't get it at all, right? He just stood there yelling at me to step away. People don't really see how things connect. They just look at the surface of everything. Like how people look at the ocean and just see water, but they don't think about all the pressure down there. 

I watched this documentary about deep-sea submarines once. The pressure is so intense it can crush a metal hull like a soda can. I used to collect soda cans when I was a kid. Mountain Dew, mostly. They had all those limited edition flavors back then, like Code Red and LiveWire. The orange one was the best. Orange is a good flavor for candy too, but not for medicine. Why do they always make children's medicine taste like fake cherries or fake oranges? It never actually tastes like the fruit. My mom used to try and hide the medicine in applesauce, but I always knew. Applesauce has that grainy texture anyway, I never really liked it. It reminds me of sand. 

So... I don't know. No, I don't think other people would get it. They just don't see how the pattern stops the rot.
Do you think the rot you're talking about is something that other people could see if it happened?

I'm not really sure if they'd see it. I mean, I never let it get that far, right? Because I always finish the sequence with the bags. But I guess... maybe? Usually, you smell rot before you see it anyway. 

Like, you know when someone leaves something in the fridge for way too long? A couple of months ago, one of the guys left this plastic container of lasagna in the station fridge. It was in there for weeks. Lasagna is a weird word to spell, actually. It has that silent 'g' in it. English is full of silent letters. Like 'knight' or 'knife'. I bought this really nice tactical knife online a while back. It has a serrated edge specifically for cutting seatbelts. You have to be super careful cutting seatbelts, though, because if you pull too hard, you can snap the blade or slip and cut the patient. We had a call once where a guy was trapped in a Honda Civic and the belt was completely jammed against the B-pillar. Hondas usually hold up pretty well in crashes, but this one was totally totaled. The windshield was basically powder. 

But... wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, the rot in the bay. Yeah, I don't know if they'd see it. I just know it would happen if I didn't finish.
Do you think the rot in the bay is something that could be prevented or stopped by anyone else, or is it only you who can prevent it?

I don't think anyone else could stop it. I mean, they sent me here because at the station I kept moving the airway bags into that exact pattern, right? I knew it was the right pattern. And I had to keep repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because it felt like the whole bay would go bad, like it would just rot, if I broke the sequence. It had to be me. 

Lieutenant Miller, he's the one who told me to stop. He has this really loud voice, like a foghorn. Foghorns are actually pretty fascinating if you think about it. They use these low-frequency sounds because low frequencies travel further through the fog than high ones. It's the same reason you can hear the bass from a car stereo from blocks away, but you can't hear the vocals until it's right next to you. My cousin had this customized Honda Civic with two massive subwoofers in the trunk. It would literally rattle the license plate right off the bumper. We used to drive around listening to techno music. Techno was huge in the late nineties. Everyone wore those wide-leg pants, JNCOs I think they were called. They were so impractical. If it rained, the bottom six inches of your pants would just soak up water like a sponge. Sponges in the ocean are actually animals, not plants, which is wild. They just sit there filtering water all day. 

But yeah, the pattern. If I didn't do it, if I didn't move the bags and say the numbers, the bay would go bad. It was up to me.
Do you think the rot in the bay would actually be visible to others if it happened, or is it something only you would know is happening?

I mean, I don't know if they'd see it. I already said I never let it get that far. But if it did happen... maybe? It would probably start in the corners, you know, where the concrete meets the wall. Concrete is so porous. That's why you have to seal it if you pour a driveway. My dad and I poured a new driveway for his house a few summers ago. It was incredibly hot work. We had to order the cement truck, and the driver was this guy who looked exactly like Hulk Hogan, minus the bandana. Wrestling was huge when I was a kid. We used to watch it every Monday night. I even had a bunch of those action figures, the ones made of that really hard rubber. If you left them out in the sun, they'd get kind of sticky. The sun degrades everything eventually. UV rays just break down the chemical bonds in plastics and rubber. That's why dashboard covers crack if you don't use a sunshade. I always use a sunshade in my car. It's one of those reflective silver ones. It folds up like an accordion. Accordions are such strange instruments. It's like a piano and a bagpipe had a baby. 

So... I don't know if they'd see the rot. Like I said, I don't let it happen.
Do you think the rot in the bay is something that could be prevented or stopped by something other than the airway bag pattern and dispatch numbers?

No, I don't think anything else would work. I mean, like I was just telling you a minute ago, that's the whole reason they sent me here in the first place. I kept moving the airway bags into that specific pattern because I knew it was the right one, and I had to keep repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. I couldn't just use something else or stop. That's why I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop, because if I broke that exact sequence, the whole bay would go bad. It had to be the bags and the dispatch numbers. 

Dispatch numbers are always so specific. Our dispatchers speak in this really flat monotone over the radio. Especially Brenda on the night shift. She drinks those massive energy drinks to stay awake, the ones with the green claw marks on the can. Energy drinks are terrible for your heart rate, honestly. Caffeine just blocks the adenosine receptors in your brain so you don't feel tired, but your body still desperately needs the rest. Sleep deprivation is actually used as an interrogation tactic by the military. The military has all sorts of crazy technology we don't even know about. Like stealth bombers. They use radar-absorbent material and special angles so they don't show up on screens. Radar was actually invented during World War II. It stands for Radio Detection and Ranging. Radios use electromagnetic waves, which are on the same spectrum as visible light, just a different frequency. Rainbows are just visible light refracting through water droplets. You can make a rainbow with a garden hose if you stand with your back to the sun. I used to do that in the backyard when I was a kid. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right. No, nothing else could stop the rot. Just the pattern.
Do you think the rot in the bay is something that would actually be there if someone else were to look, even if you weren't thinking about it?

I mean, I don't know if they'd see it because, like I keep saying, I never let it happen. That's why they brought me here in the first place, right? Because I wouldn't let it happen. I was at the station, and I was moving the airway bags into that pattern—the pattern I knew was right—and I had to keep repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. I couldn't stop. My lieutenant told me to step away, but I couldn't, because if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would just rot. 

But you know, thinking about it... if I wasn't thinking about it, I guess I'd be asleep. Sleep is so weird, isn't it? Your brain just cycles through these different stages, like REM sleep where you dream. I read somewhere that you only dream for a few minutes at a time, even if it feels like hours. My dreams are usually in color, but I heard some people only dream in black and white. That reminds me of those old black-and-white TVs. My grandparents had one in their basement when I was little. It had these big clunky dials you had to turn to change the channel. There were only like, three channels anyway. You always had to mess with the rabbit ear antennas to get the static to go away. Static electricity is what happens when you rub a balloon on your hair. It makes your hair stand straight up. Hair is actually just dead cells. It's crazy that we spend so much money cutting and styling something that isn't even alive. Barbershops always smell like that blue liquid they keep the combs in. Barbicide, I think it's called. 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, if someone else looked. I don't know. I just know I had to do the pattern with the bags and the numbers so it wouldn't happen.
Do you think the rot in the bay would still be a problem if you weren't there to think about it?

I mean, I don't know, because I was there. That's the whole thing, right? Like I keep telling you, that's why they sent me to this place. I was at the station, and I had to keep moving the airway bags into that exact pattern, the one I knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. I had to do it. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop, to step away, but I couldn't. If I broke that sequence, the whole bay was going to go bad. It would just rot. 

But if I wasn't there... I don't know. Being there is the only way you can affect things. Like when you're driving an ambulance. You have to be in the driver's seat to steer it. The steering wheels on those rigs are huge, much bigger than a regular car. They have to be, to turn those massive tires. Tires are made of vulcanized rubber. Charles Goodyear invented that process. He accidentally dropped rubber and sulfur on a hot stove. It's funny how many inventions are just accidents. Like penicillin. Alexander Fleming just left a petri dish out and mold grew on it. Mold is a type of fungus. Fungi are more closely related to animals than plants, which is really weird to think about. Mushrooms are fungi. Some mushrooms are poisonous, but some are delicious. I like the little white button mushrooms on pizza. Pizza is probably the best food ever invented. The Italians really nailed that one. 

Anyway... I don't know what would happen if I wasn't there. I just know I had to keep the sequence going.
Do you think the rot in the bay is something that would still exist even if nobody, including you, believed in it or thought about it?

I mean, I don't really know if it would still be there, because I believed in it, you know? I was thinking about it. Like I've been saying, that's why I'm even in this place. I was at the station, and I had all the airway bags out, and I was moving them into this specific pattern. I just knew it was the right pattern. And I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over. I had to. My lieutenant came over and told me to stop and step away, but I couldn't do it. If I stopped, if I broke that sequence, the whole bay was going to go bad. It was going to rot. 

But if nobody believed in it... belief is a powerful thing. People believe in all kinds of stuff, like ghosts or aliens. I saw this documentary once about the Roswell crash in 1947. They said it was a weather balloon, but weather balloons don't leave metallic debris that you can't cut or burn. Weather balloons are usually made of latex or neoprene. Latex comes from rubber trees. They tap the trees kind of like how you tap maple trees for syrup. Maple syrup is so much better than that fake corn syrup stuff they sell in the plastic bottles shaped like a lady. Corn syrup is in everything now, though. It's why everyone is getting diabetes. The pancreas just gives out. The pancreas is this weird little organ tucked behind the stomach. It looks kind of like a lumpy tongue. 

What were you asking me? Oh, about the rot. Yeah, I don't know what would happen if nobody thought about it. I just know I had to keep the bags and the numbers going.
Do you think the rot in the bay would still exist if you weren't thinking about it and nobody else believed in it?

Look, doc, I don't know how many different ways I can explain this to you. I was there, so I was thinking about it. That's the whole reason I'm stuck in this place. Like I keep saying, at the station, I was moving the airway bags into that exact pattern, the one that I just knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. I couldn't just stop. The lieutenant kept telling me to step back, but I couldn't do it, because if I broke that sequence, the whole bay was gonna go bad. It would rot. 

But if nobody believed it... I mean, belief is just... it's like believing the expiration dates on the saline flushes we carry. You throw them out, but salt and water don't actually expire. The ocean is just salt water, and it's been around for billions of years. The Pacific is the biggest. It has the Mariana Trench, which is so deep you could drop Mount Everest into it and it would still be totally underwater. Mount Everest is in Nepal, I think. People pay crazy money to climb it, and they just leave their empty oxygen bottles all over the mountain. Oxygen is dangerous, you know. We have to be so careful with the O2 tanks in the back of the rig. If you drop a D-cylinder and the valve snaps off, the thing turns into a literal torpedo. It'll punch a hole straight through a cinderblock wall. Cinderblocks are so heavy. They use them to build foundations. My uncle built his own shed out of them once, but he didn't mix the mortar right, so it always leaked when it rained... 

Wait, what did you just ask me? Something about the bags?
Do you think the rot in the bay would still exist if nobody, including you, was thinking about it or talking about it, and there was no evidence of it anywhere?

I don't... I don't really get why you keep asking me the exact same thing, doc. It's like you're not listening to me. If nobody was thinking about it and there was no evidence... I mean, I guess it wouldn't exist? But I *was* thinking about it. I was right there in the bay. I had to arrange the airway bags. I had the sequence in my head, the dispatch numbers, and I was saying them out loud. If I stopped, the rot was going to happen. My lieutenant didn't get it, he just told me to stop, but I knew what would happen if I did. 

Evidence is a tricky thing, though. Like, what even counts as evidence? In court, they use DNA now, but before that, it was just fingerprints. Fingerprints are weird. No two people have the same ones, not even identical twins. Twins happen when a single egg splits, or when two eggs get fertilized at the same time. Fraternal twins can be a boy and a girl. I went to high school with fraternal twins, Mark and Sarah. Mark drove this beat-up old Chevy Nova. Chevy doesn't make the Nova anymore. The story goes that they couldn't sell it in Spanish-speaking countries because "no va" means "it doesn't go," but that's actually an urban legend. People believe so many urban legends. Like the one about the guy waking up in a bathtub full of ice with his kidney missing. Kidneys filter your blood. You only really need one to live, which is why people can donate them. Donating an organ is a huge deal. You have to go under general anesthesia. Anesthesia is basically controlled poisoning... 

I'm sorry, I forgot what we were talking about. Did you ask me about the station again?
Do you think the rot in the bay would still be there if everyone, including you, forgot about it and never thought about it again?

Are you messing with me, doc? Because I swear you're asking me the exact same thing again. If everyone forgot about it... I mean, if it's completely forgotten, then maybe it's not there. But I didn't forget. I couldn't. I was right there in the middle of it. That's why they sent me to this place, because I was at the station, and I had all the airway bags out, and I kept moving them into this specific pattern. I just knew it was the right pattern. And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over. My lieutenant was yelling at me to step away, to stop, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't. If I broke that sequence, the whole bay was gonna go bad. It was going to rot. 

But forgetting things... memory is a weird thing, isn't it? Like, how do you know if a memory is even real? Sometimes people have false memories. There was this whole thing in the 80s or 90s, the Satanic Panic, where people thought all these daycares were doing crazy rituals, but it was just kids being led by therapists to say things. Therapy can be really dangerous if you get the wrong person. They can put ideas in your head. Like inception. That movie with Leonardo DiCaprio. He was also in Titanic. The Titanic sank because they ignored the ice warnings. Icebergs are mostly underwater, you only see the very top of them. That's why they're so dangerous to ships. Ships use sonar now to see what's under the water. Sonar uses sound waves. Bats use something like that, echolocation, to catch bugs in the dark. Bats can eat like a thousand mosquitoes in an hour. Mosquitoes are the deadliest animal on earth because they carry malaria. Malaria... wait. 

What did you ask me? Did you ask about the airway bags again?
Do you think the rot in the bay would still be a problem if someone else were to take over your responsibilities and arrange the airway bags in a different pattern?

No, no, they couldn't do that. Someone else couldn't take over, because they wouldn't know the pattern. That's why I was doing it. I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern that I *knew* was right, and I had to say the dispatch numbers out loud. If someone else did it, they'd mess up the sequence, and the whole bay would rot. My lieutenant just didn't understand, he kept telling me to stop and step away, but I couldn't. I couldn't break the sequence. That's why they sent me here, because I wouldn't stop. 

But taking over responsibilities... it's like when you have a substitute teacher. They never know the lesson plan. In fourth grade, we had this sub, Mr. Peterson, and he just let us watch Bill Nye the Science Guy all day. Bill Nye always wore bow ties. Bow ties are really hard to tie, you have to watch a YouTube video to figure it out. YouTube has a video for everything now. You can learn how to fix a leaky faucet or build a whole house. Houses are so expensive right now, the interest rates are crazy. Banks control the interest rates, and they just keep printing more money. Paper money isn't even backed by gold anymore, it's just fiat currency. Gold is really heavy, though. Like, in the movies when they steal gold bars and just toss them in a duffel bag? That's totally fake. A standard gold bar weighs like 27 pounds. You couldn't carry a whole bag of them. You'd throw your back out. Back injuries are the worst in EMS, you know. We have to use power stretchers now to save our backs. Stretchers... 

Wait, did you ask me about the stretchers? Or the bags again?
Do you think the rot in the bay would still be there if you weren't thinking about it and nobody else believed in it, and there was no other evidence of it?

I... doc, why do you keep asking me the exact same thing? It's like you're stuck on a loop. If I wasn't thinking about it and nobody believed in it... I mean, I don't know, maybe? But I *was* thinking about it. I was right there. I've told you this. They sent me to this place because I was at the station, and I had the airway bags, and I kept moving them into this pattern. I just knew it was the right pattern. And I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't. I couldn't break the sequence, or the whole bay was gonna go bad and rot. 

But believing in things... belief is powerful. People believe in ghosts, you know? Like poltergeists that move things around. There's this famous one, the Bell Witch. It supposedly haunted this family in Tennessee way back in the 1800s. Tennessee is famous for whiskey. Jack Daniel's is made there, in a dry county, which is super ironic. You can't even buy it where they make it. Kind of like how the guy who invented the stop sign never learned how to drive. Driving in the city is a nightmare anyway, the traffic lights are never synced up. They use algorithms for traffic lights now. Algorithms run everything, like your social media feed. It just feeds you what you want to see. It's like an echo chamber. Echos happen when sound bounces off a hard surface, like in a canyon. The Grand Canyon is huge, it took the Colorado River millions of years to carve it out. Rivers are fresh water, but the ocean is salt water. Salt makes you float better, like in the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea is so salty nothing can live in it...

Wait, did you ask me about the ocean? Or the airway bags again?
Do you think the rot in the bay is something that exists independently of your thoughts about it?

Are you kidding me right now? Independently of my thoughts? Doc, I feel like a broken record here, you are literally asking me the exact same thing again. It's not just a thought! That's exactly why they sent me to this place. I was at the station, and I kept moving the airway bags into this pattern because I *knew* it was the right one. I had to do it. And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant was yelling at me to step away and stop, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't! Because I knew if I broke the sequence, the whole bay was gonna go bad and rot. It's not just some thought in my head. 

But speaking of heads, the human brain is crazy, right? It's basically just a lump of fat and electricity. Electricity is how everything works now. Even cars. Electric cars are everywhere, but the batteries are a huge hazard for us in EMS. If an EV catches fire, you can't just put it out with water, it burns for days. Firefighters absolutely hate them. Fire is actually a chemical reaction, you know, it needs oxygen, heat, and fuel. The fire triangle. Triangles are the strongest shape in architecture. That's why bridges use trusses. The Golden Gate Bridge is painted International Orange, not red. Orange is a weird color, nothing really rhymes with it. Well, maybe door hinge, if you say it fast. Eminem did that once in an interview. Eminem is from Detroit. Detroit used to be the motor city, but then all the factories closed down and people just left. Abandoned buildings everywhere. Urban explorers love that stuff, they go in with flashlights and take pictures of the decay. Flashlights used to take those huge D batteries, but now everything is LED and rechargeable. Lithium-ion... 

Wait. What were you asking me? Were we talking about the batteries? Or the bay again?
Do you think the rot in the bay would still exist if you weren't thinking about it and there was no evidence of it, or is it something that only happens because you believe in it?

Doc, seriously, are you messing with me? This is like the fourth time you've asked the exact same thing! "Only happens because I believe it"—no, I keep telling you what actually happened. That is the exact reason they sent me here in the first place! I was at the station, and I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern I knew was right. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't do it. Because if I broke the sequence, I felt like the whole bay was gonna go bad and rot. It's about the sequence, not just me thinking about it. 

Sequences are how the whole universe is held together. Like the Fibonacci sequence. You see it in sunflowers and pinecones. Pinecones have seeds inside them, and squirrels stash them for winter. Winter is getting warmer every year, though, because of the greenhouse effect. Greenhouses are made of glass, obviously, but glass is actually a liquid, not a solid. It just flows really, really slowly. That's why really old windows are thicker at the bottom. Stained glass windows in cathedrals are amazing, especially the blue ones. They use cobalt to make the glass blue. Cobalt is mined for phone batteries now. Everyone is just addicted to their phones, staring at screens all day, totally ruining their posture. Chiropractors make an absolute fortune cracking people's necks. I hate the sound of a neck cracking, man. It sounds exactly like stepping on a dry branch in the woods. The woods at night are actually really loud with all the crickets. Crickets rub their legs together to make that chirping sound, they don't even have vocal cords...

Wait. What did you just ask me? Were we talking about the crickets? Or the airway bags again?
Do you think the rot in the bay would still exist if you weren't thinking about it and there was no evidence of it?

Doc, is this a joke? Are you testing my memory or something? I feel like I'm losing my mind here, you just asked me that exact same question! I don't know what happens if I wasn't thinking about it, because I *was* thinking about it! That's the whole reason I'm locked up in here. I was at the station, and I was moving the airway bags into the right pattern, repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant was literally yelling at me to step away, but I couldn't stop. I knew if I broke that sequence, the whole bay was gonna rot. 

Speaking of the bay, bays are usually connected to the ocean, right? The ocean has tides, which are controlled by the moon's gravity. Gravity is just the bending of spacetime, according to Einstein. Einstein had crazy hair. He never wore socks, either. Did you know that? He thought socks were a waste of time because they always get holes in them. Holes in your socks are the absolute worst, especially when you have to wear heavy steel-toe boots for a 12-hour shift on the rig. EMT boots have to be tough. Leather is best, but you have to polish it. Shoe polish smells like harsh chemicals. Chemicals are everywhere now, in our food, in the water. They put fluoride in the tap water to protect our teeth, but some people think it's for mind control. It calcifies the pineal gland, right? It's this thing shaped like a tiny pinecone right in the dead center of your brain. Descartes thought it was the seat of the human soul. The soul supposedly weighs 21 grams. There was a movie about that a long time ago. Movies used to be shot on actual film, celluloid. It was highly flammable. If it caught fire in the projector room, the whole theater could burn down in minutes. Movie theaters always have those sticky floors from the spilled soda. Soda has way too much high fructose corn syrup in it now, it's why everyone has diabetes... 

Hold on. What did you just ask me? Were we talking about the movie theaters? Or the airway bags again?
